adjudication_records.issue_text: app/mailers/user_notifications.rb:295 — [P1, confidence 100] `unsubscribe_url: post.topic.unsubscribe_url,` — Every recipient gets the same topic-only URL, so the action cannot identify the emailed user and instead changes whichever account owns the browser session, leaving the intended recipient subscribed whenever those identities differ.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a security/functionality issue. Looking at the diff, the unsubscribe_url is set to `post.topic.unsubscribe_url` which returns just `"#{url}/unsubscribe"` (a topic-only URL with no user identifier). The topics_controller.rb unsubscribe action uses `current_user` to find the TopicUser record, meaning it operates on whoever is logged in when clicking the link, not necessarily the email recipient. This is a real bug - if user A receives an email and user B clicks the link while logged in, user B's subscription changes instead of user A's.

adjudication_records.issue_text: config/routes.rb:440 — [P1, confidence 100] `get "t/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe" => "topics#unsubscribe", constraints: {topic_id: /\d+/}` — Dereferencing an email URL performs a non-idempotent preference write, so mail-client prefetchers, link checkers, and ordinary reloads unsubscribe or further mute users without an explicit state-change command.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows a new GET route at 't/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe' that maps to 'topics#unsubscribe'. Looking at the controller code in app/controllers/topics_controller.rb, the unsubscribe action performs a write operation - it modifies the TopicUser notification_level and calls tu.save!. This is a non-idempotent state change triggered by a GET request. Email clients, link prefetchers, and security scanners commonly make GET requests to URLs in emails, which would unintentionally change user notification preferences. This is a real bug - GET requests should be idempotent per HTTP semantics, but this endpoint modifies user state.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/controllers/topics_controller.rb:113 — [P2, confidence 100] `tu.save!` — This writes `notification_level` outside `TopicUser.change`, leaving `notifications_changed_at` and `notifications_reason_id` stale and omitting the MessageBus publication, so automatic notification policy and other live clients observe contradictory state.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that in the new `unsubscribe` action (lines 98-117), `tu.save!` is called directly on the TopicUser record after modifying `notification_level`. Looking at the `TopicUser.change` method shown in the diff (around line 113-115), it includes `MessageBus.publish` for notification_level changes. The direct `tu.save!` bypasses this, meaning the MessageBus publication won't happen and other fields that `TopicUser.change` might update (like `notifications_changed_at`) won't be set. This is a real consistency issue where the unsubscribe action doesn't follow the established pattern for changing notification levels.

adjudication_records.issue_text: config/locales/server.en.yml:1855 — [P2, confidence 100] `To stop receiving notifications about this particular topic, [click here](%{unsubscribe_url}).` — The global `unsubscribe_link` template now unconditionally requires topic-specific data, so every non-topic caller of the existing generic `add_unsubscribe_link` MessageBuilder contract becomes invalid.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that the `unsubscribe_link` template in server.en.yml now includes `%{unsubscribe_url}` which requires topic-specific data. Looking at lib/email/message_builder.rb, the `html_part` method calls `I18n.t('unsubscribe_link', template_args)` when `add_unsubscribe_link` is true. The `template_args` only includes `unsubscribe_url` if it was passed in `@opts`. In user_notifications.rb, the `unsubscribe_url` is only added for topic notification emails (`unsubscribe_url: post.topic.unsubscribe_url`). Any other email that uses `add_unsubscribe_link: true` without providing `unsubscribe_url` will now have a broken/missing interpolation in the unsubscribe message. This is a real bug where the global template now requires data that not all callers provide.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/controllers/topics_controller.rb:99 — [P2, confidence 75] `@topic_view = TopicView.new(params[:topic_id], current_user)` — At email-click volume this preference command materializes and serializes a full topic view although its page consumes only title and notification state, and replacing `TopicView` with a lightweight topic projection preserves the selector UI while deleting the post-stream query and serialization fanout.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the new `unsubscribe` action in topics_controller.rb creates a full TopicView object (`@topic_view = TopicView.new(params[:topic_id], current_user)`) and then calls `perform_show_response` which serializes the entire topic. Looking at the template (topic/unsubscribe.hbs), it only uses `stopNotificiationsText` (which needs title) and `topic-notifications-button`. This is a legitimate performance/architecture concern - the unsubscribe page loads a full topic view when it only needs minimal data. However, this is an optimization suggestion rather than a bug - the code will function correctly, just inefficiently. The finding is grounded in specific diff code and represents a valid architectural concern for a feature designed to handle email-click volume.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/mailers/user_notifications.rb:295 — [P1, confidence 100] `unsubscribe_url: post.topic.unsubscribe_url,` — Every recipient receives the same topic-only URL, so a recipient who opens the email while signed into another account unsubscribes that other account through `current_user` and remains subscribed on the account that received the email.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a security issue. Looking at the diff, the unsubscribe_url is set to `post.topic.unsubscribe_url` which generates a URL like `/t/slug/id/unsubscribe`. In the topics_controller.rb, the `unsubscribe` action uses `current_user` to find and modify the TopicUser record: `tu = TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id])`. This means if user A receives an email but user B is logged in when clicking the link, user B's subscription will be modified, not user A's. The URL contains no user-specific token to verify the intended recipient.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/controllers/topics_controller.rb:107 — [P1, confidence 75] `if tu.notification_level > TopicUser.notification_levels[:regular]` — A mailing-list recipient who is tracking or watching is reduced only to `regular` rather than `muted`, so the mailing-list notification path continues emailing every post from the topic after the advertised unsubscribe action.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies the logic in the unsubscribe action at lines 104-110. When a user clicks unsubscribe, if their notification_level is > regular (i.e., tracking or watching), it only reduces to 'regular' level, not 'muted'. The 'regular' level still receives notifications for @mentions and replies. This means users who were watching/tracking a topic and click 'unsubscribe' will still receive some notifications, which contradicts the expected behavior of an unsubscribe action. The email template says 'stop receiving notifications' but the implementation only partially reduces notification level.

Looking at the diff for topic_user.rb, the `change` method handles additional logic including publishing MessageBus notifications and properly updating records. The direct assignment in the unsubscribe controller (lines 103-108) bypasses this, which means `notifications_reason_id` won't be cleared and `notifications_changed_at` won't be updated. adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real security issue. adjudication_records.issue_text: app/controllers/topics_controller.rb:107 — [P1, confidence 100] `if tu.notification_level > TopicUser.notification_levels[:regular]` — Retrying the same GET after a lost response or reloading it changes a watching/tracking topic to `regular` on the first request and then to `muted` on the second, so duplicate delivery silently applies a stronger state than the acknowledged request and the unsubscribe label does not make the transition idempotent.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a real issue in the unsubscribe action. Looking at lines 103-111 of topics_controller.rb, the logic is: if notification_level > regular, set to regular; else set to muted. This means a GET request to /unsubscribe is not idempotent - the first request changes watching/tracking to regular, and a second request (e.g., page reload, retry after network issue) would change regular to muted. This is a legitimate bug where duplicate GET requests cause progressively stronger notification suppression than intended.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows the new `unsubscribe` action in topics_controller.rb at line 105 does `tu = TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id])` and then immediately accesses `tu.notification_level` on line 107 without any nil check. If a user visits the unsubscribe URL but has no TopicUser record (e.g., they never visited the topic, or it's a different account than the one that received the email), `tu` will be nil and `tu.notification_level` will raise a NoMethodError. This is a real bug - the code assumes a TopicUser record always exists but that's not guaranteed.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/controllers/topics_controller.rb:113 — [P2, confidence 75] `tu.save!` — When a notification-setting request commits after this action has read `tu` but before this stale instance saves, the delayed save overwrites the newer explicit setting and leaves the UI/account state desynchronized, because this read-modify-write has neither row locking nor an optimistic-lock version check.

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real race condition in the new `unsubscribe` action. The code reads a TopicUser record, modifies its notification_level in memory, then saves it. Between the read and save, another request could modify the same record, and this save would overwrite those changes. The diff shows no locking mechanism (pessimistic or optimistic) to prevent this. While this is a low-probability race condition in practice, it is a valid concurrency bug in the new code.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows a new GET route 'get "t/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe" => "topics#unsubscribe"' that performs a state-changing action (modifying notification_level in TopicUser and calling tu.save!). The controller action is added to skip_before_filter :check_xhr but still requires login. However, GET requests in Rails don't have CSRF protection by default, and the action modifies user state.
